learning_activity_name: Describe the principles and practices for the production of selected crops (mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew)
sla_name: Production of mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew
sla_assessment_criteria: The principles and practices applied in the production of selected crops (mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew) are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Fields of the selected crops|Common tools/ equipment|Materials/ supplies used in production of the selected crops|Units/agencies carrying out various activities involved in value chain of the selected crops
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Selected cash and horticultural crops are grown for income, food and export. Each crop has its own climate, soil, propagation and management needs.
sla_notes_details: Mushroom is a fungus grown indoors on a substrate such as straw, sawdust or maize cobs that is pasteurised, inoculated with spawn, incubated in the dark and then fruited in humid, ventilated rooms at about 20 to 28 degrees C. Clove is a tropical tree grown on well-drained soils in humid coastal areas (Zanzibar and Pemba), propagated by seed, harvested as unopened flower buds and dried. Avocado is grown from grafted seedlings in deep, well-drained soils, spaced about 8 to 10 metres apart, with mulching and pruning. Tea and coffee are grown in highland areas with adequate rainfall: tea is propagated by cuttings and plucked regularly, while Arabica coffee needs 1000 to 2000 mm of rainfall and altitude of 1000 to 2000 m and is pruned, mulched and harvested as ripe cherries. Cashew grows best in coastal areas with sandy soils and 500 to 1500 mm of rainfall and is propagated by seed or grafting.
sla_notes_illustrations: A farmer in Kilimanjaro plants Arabica coffee seedlings at 2.7 m by 2.7 m in holes prepared with manure, mulches to keep moisture and prunes the trees after harvest to maintain yields.
sla_notes_daily_life: These crops provide household income, employment and export earnings, and mushrooms and avocados supply nutritious food to families.
sla_exercise: Name the growing medium commonly used for mushroom production.::A pasteurised substrate such as straw, sawdust or maize cobs.||Which part of the clove plant is harvested and sold?::The unopened flower buds.||State two climatic requirements of Arabica coffee.::Adequate rainfall (1000 to 2000 mm) and cool highland altitude (1000 to 2000 m).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the principles of agriculture
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate a basic understanding of the agricultural value chain for selected products
learning_activity_name: Analyse the problems associated with the cultivation, postharvest management and marketing of selected crops (mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew) and propose possible solutions
sla_name: Problems in cultivation, postharvest management and marketing of mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew
sla_assessment_criteria: The problems associated with cultivation, postharvest management and marketing of the selected crops (mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew) are well analysed and possible solutions proposed.
sla_teaching_aids: Fields of the selected crops|Units/ agencies carrying out various activities involved in value chain of the selected crops
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Producers of these crops meet challenges at every stage, from the field to the market. Analysing them helps find practical solutions.
sla_notes_details: Cultivation problems include pests and diseases (for example coffee berry disease and leaf rust, tea blister blight and cashew powdery mildew), poor planting material, drought and high input costs. Postharvest problems include bruising and rapid spoilage of avocados and mushrooms, poor drying of cloves and cashew nuts that causes mould, inadequate storage and lack of processing facilities, which lead to losses. Marketing problems include unstable prices, weak farmer organisation, poor roads, few buyers and dependence on raw exports. Possible solutions are using certified seedlings and integrated pest management, training in proper harvesting and drying, cold storage and packaging, forming cooperatives, adding value by processing, and using market information systems.
sla_notes_illustrations: Cashew farmers who dry nuts on clean raised platforms and sell through a cooperative obtain higher grade and prices than those who sell wet nuts to individual middlemen.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers reduce postharvest losses and earn more when they harvest at the right stage, store well and sell together, which improves family incomes.
sla_exercise: Give two postharvest problems of avocado.::Bruising and rapid spoilage or over-ripening.||How can farmers reduce the market problem of low prices for their crops?::By forming cooperatives, processing to add value and using market information.||Name one disease of coffee.::Coffee berry disease (or coffee leaf rust).

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of some advanced technologies in agriculture
learning_activity_name: Describe advanced agricultural technologies used in crop production (technologies used in planning, site selection, propagation and nursery management, crop establishment, crop management, postharvest management, and marketing)
sla_name: Advanced agricultural technologies used in crop production
sla_assessment_criteria: Advanced agricultural technologies used in crop production (technologies used in planning, site selection, propagation and nursery management, crop establishment, crop management, postharvest management, and marketing) are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Fields of various crops|Units/agencies carrying out various activities involved in value chain of crops|Tools/equipment & materials/ supplies for crop production
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Advanced technologies increase the efficiency, quality and profitability of crop production at all stages of the value chain.
sla_notes_details: In planning and site selection, tools such as soil testing kits, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), GPS and weather data are used to choose suitable land. In propagation and nursery management, technologies include tissue culture, grafting, seedling trays, shade nets and mist propagation. In crop establishment and management, they include drip and sprinkler irrigation, fertigation, precision planting, greenhouses, integrated pest management, drones for spraying and monitoring, and mobile applications for advice. Postharvest technologies include solar dryers, cold rooms, improved storage bags, grading and packing machines. Marketing technologies include mobile money, e-commerce and market information through phones.
sla_notes_illustrations: A horticulture farmer uses drip irrigation with fertigation in a greenhouse to grow tomatoes, saving water and increasing yield per square metre compared with open-field watering by hand.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers who use phones for weather and price information, and simple tools such as solar dryers, reduce risks and increase income.
sla_exercise: State one technology used to propagate plants quickly and disease-free.::Tissue culture.||What is the advantage of drip irrigation?::It saves water by delivering it directly to the plant roots.||Name one postharvest technology for drying crops.::A solar dryer.

main_competence_name: Use some advanced technologies in agriculture
specific_competence_name: Use technology to increase agricultural production
learning_activity_name: Apply basic and some advanced agricultural technologies in the production of selected crops (mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew)
sla_name: Applying basic and advanced technologies in producing mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew
sla_assessment_criteria: Advanced agricultural technologies in the production of the selected crops (mushroom, clove, avocado, tea, coffee and cashew) are well applied.
sla_teaching_aids: Tools/equipment & materials/ supplies used in the production of mushroom|Clove|Avocado|Tea|Coffee|Cashew
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students practise the production of selected crops using both basic and advanced technologies at the school or home farm.
sla_notes_details: The practical steps include site selection and preparation, preparing planting material (spawn and substrate for mushroom, seedlings and grafts for tree crops), planting at the recommended spacing, mulching, manuring, irrigation, weeding, pruning, pest and disease control, harvesting at the right maturity and postharvest handling. Students record activities in a farm record book, implement affordable solutions to problems such as drought or diseases (for example mulching, use of resistant varieties, botanical pesticides), and try out and adapt technologies like drip irrigation, grafting and solar drying. Safety rules are observed when using tools and chemicals.
sla_notes_illustrations: Students graft avocado seedlings, plant them in prepared holes at 8 m spacing with compost, install a simple drip line made from bottles and record growth every month.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skills prepare students to start small farms or agribusinesses and to advise their families and neighbours.
sla_exercise: Why are records kept during crop production?::To monitor activities, costs, yields and profit and to plan better.||Give one affordable method of conserving soil moisture.::Mulching.||State one safety rule when using pesticides.::Wear protective clothing and follow label instructions.

learning_activity_name: Identify agricultural problem in society, and design and carry out a project to address it
sla_name: Agricultural project: identifying a problem and starting a project
sla_assessment_criteria: Agricultural problem in society identified, and a project to address it is well designed and implementation started.
sla_teaching_aids: Various tools|Equipment & supplies|Reports related to the chosen project
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A project is a planned activity carried out to solve a real agricultural problem in society.
sla_notes_details: Students identify a problem in any part of the crop or animal value chain, such as low yields, poor postharvest storage or lack of markets, by observation and interviewing farmers. They then state objectives, choose a suitable project idea, make a plan covering activities, resources, timeline, costs and expected income, and begin implementation. Records of activities and expenses are kept, and risks and ways of managing them are considered.
sla_notes_illustrations: Students in a village where tomatoes rot after harvest plan a project to build and test a simple solar dryer, listing materials, costs and dates, and begin construction.
sla_notes_daily_life: Projects give students practical experience in solving community problems and can develop into small businesses.
sla_exercise: List two steps in starting an agricultural project.::Identify the problem and plan the activities, resources and costs.||Why should a project have a budget?::To estimate the costs and income and to manage resources.||Where can students get information to identify the problem?::By observation, interviews with farmers and surveys.

sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: These are important industrial and cash crops in Tanzania, and each has specific requirements and practices.
sla_notes_details: Cotton is grown in the Lake Zone on well-drained fertile soils with 500 to 1000 mm of rain, planted at the start of rains in rows, thinned, weeded, sprayed against bollworms and harvested by hand as bolls open. Oil palm grows in the humid lowlands of Kigoma with high rainfall, is propagated from certified seedlings from nurseries, planted at about 9 m spacing in triangles, fertilised and harvested as fresh fruit bunches. Sisal grows in hot, dry areas on well-drained soils, propagated by bulbils or suckers and its leaves are cut for fibre. Coconut grows in coastal areas with sandy soils, raised from seed nuts in nurseries and planted at about 7.5 to 9 m spacing. Grape is grown in Dodoma and Singida on well-drained soils with plenty of sunshine, propagated by cuttings, trained on trellises and pruned annually to produce fruit.
sla_notes_illustrations: A Shinyanga cotton farmer plants seed at 90 cm by 30 cm after the first rains, thins to one plant per hole, and sprays three times to protect the crop from bollworms.
sla_notes_daily_life: These crops provide income, cooking oil, fibre, drinks and food, and create jobs in processing factories and markets.
sla_exercise: Name the product obtained from oil palm.::Palm oil from fresh fruit bunches.||How is sisal commonly propagated?::By bulbils or suckers.||Why are grape vines trained on trellises?::To support the vines, expose them to sunlight and make pruning and harvesting easier.

sla_assessment_criteria: Basic principles and some advanced practices for production of goat and sheep are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Production guides|Tools/equipment|Materials for production of goat|Sheep|Goat|Sheep rearing units
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Goats and sheep are small ruminants kept for meat, milk, mohair and wool, and they are suited to many farming systems.
sla_notes_details: Breeds include meat goats (Small East African, Boer), dairy goats (Toggenburg, Saanen), mohair goats (Angora), meat sheep (Blackhead Persian, Red Maasai) and woollen sheep (Merino, Corriedale). Practices include selecting breeding stock, housing in well-ventilated raised pens, feeding on pasture, browse, hay and supplements with mineral licks and clean water, controlling parasites by dipping, spraying and drenching, vaccinating against diseases such as PPR and foot and mouth disease, breeding management with a buck or ram to about 20 females, kidding or lambing care, and record keeping. Wool is shorn once or twice a year and dairy goats are milked twice daily.
sla_notes_illustrations: A farmer keeps 20 Small East African does and one Boer buck in a raised slatted house, gives hay and mineral blocks in the dry season, and drenches every three months.
sla_notes_daily_life: Small ruminants give households meat, milk and income and need less land and capital than cattle.
sla_exercise: Name one breed of dairy goat.::Toggenburg (or Saanen).||Which product is obtained from Angora goats?::Mohair.||State one disease that is controlled by vaccination in goats and sheep.::Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) or foot and mouth disease.

sla_assessment_criteria: Problems associated with the cultivation, postharvest management and marketing of the selected crops (cotton, oil palm, sisal, coconut and grape) are well analysed, and possible solutions proposed.
sla_teaching_aids: Fields for production of cotton|Oil palm|Sisal|Coconut|Grape|Documentaries depicting problems in various segments of value chains in production of the selected crops|Their solutions

sla_notes_intro: Producers of these crops meet challenges in the field, after harvest and at the market, and solutions must be proposed.
sla_notes_details: Cultivation problems include bollworms and other pests in cotton, lethal yellowing and pests in coconut, fungal diseases in grape, shortage of quality seedlings, drought and land conflicts. Postharvest problems include mixing cotton grades, contamination and delays in processing oil palm bunches, poor drying of coconut copra, and fruit spoilage in grape. Marketing problems include low and unstable prices, few processors, poor infrastructure, high transport costs and weak bargaining power of farmers. Possible solutions are using certified seed and integrated pest management, grading and clean handling, building local processing plants, farmer cooperatives, contract farming, and value addition such as making oil, juice, wine and rope.
sla_notes_illustrations: Grape farmers in Dodoma who sell fruit to a local winery through a cooperative obtain a more stable price than those who sell fresh grapes by the roadside.
sla_notes_daily_life: Solving these problems raises farmers' incomes and reduces losses, and it supports local industries and jobs.
sla_exercise: Give one problem in cotton production.::Bollworm attack (or low prices).||Suggest one way to add value to coconut.::Process into coconut oil, copra or coir products.||How can cooperatives help farmers in marketing?::By selling in bulk, negotiating better prices and reducing transport costs.

sla_assessment_criteria: Problems associated with husbandry, postharvest management and marketing of livestock produce and products (goat & sheep) are well analysed and viable solutions proposed.

sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Goat and sheep farmers face problems in husbandry, in handling produce after production and in marketing.
sla_notes_details: Husbandry problems include diseases and parasites, shortage of feed in the dry season, poor breeds, inbreeding and predators. Postharvest problems relate to poor slaughter and meat hygiene, milk spoilage due to lack of cooling, and poor wool or skin handling that lowers quality. Marketing problems include unreliable market information, long distances to markets, poor transport, low prices, and middlemen. Proposed solutions include vaccination and regular dipping, feed conservation as hay and silage, crossbreeding, hygienic slaughter and milk handling, cooling and pasteurisation, grading of skins, forming marketing groups, and using livestock auction markets and mobile phone price information.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group of goat keepers builds a milk collection centre with a cooler, so milk from many members is sold each morning to a dairy at a fixed price.
sla_notes_daily_life: Solving these problems allows families to earn steady income and to supply safe, quality meat and milk to communities.
sla_exercise: State two feed conservation methods for the dry season.::Making hay and silage.||Why is milk cooling important?::It slows bacterial growth and prevents spoilage.||How can goat farmers avoid inbreeding?::By exchanging breeding males or bringing in new males from other flocks.

learning_activity_name: Describe advanced agricultural technologies used in animal production (technologies in husbandry, postharvest management and marketing)
sla_name: Advanced agricultural technologies used in animal production
sla_assessment_criteria: Advanced agricultural technologies used in animal production (technologies in husbandry, postharvest management and marketing) are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Documentaries depicting application of advanced technologies in various segments of value chains in animal production
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Advanced technologies improve the productivity, health and value of animals and animal products.
sla_notes_details: In husbandry, technologies include artificial insemination, embryo transfer, improved breeds, computerised feeding systems, automatic waterers, electronic identification, milking machines, and mobile applications for herd records and health alerts. In postharvest management, they include milk coolers and pasteurisers, hygienic abattoirs, cold-chain transport, and preservation of meat by refrigeration, drying and smoking. In marketing, they include online livestock markets, mobile money, traceability systems and e-commerce for meat and dairy products. Methods such as demonstrations and field visits show how these can be adapted to small farms.
sla_notes_illustrations: A dairy goat farmer uses artificial insemination with semen from a high-yielding buck to improve the herd and records milk yield on a phone application.
sla_notes_daily_life: Technologies help small livestock keepers increase output, protect animal health and access wider markets.
sla_exercise: What is artificial insemination?::Placing collected semen into the female's reproductive tract using instruments instead of natural mating.||Name one technology for keeping milk fresh.::A milk cooler (refrigeration) or pasteuriser.||How can mobile phones help livestock keepers?::They provide market prices, weather and health information and allow mobile money payments.

sla_notes_intro: Students perform practical production of selected industrial crops using basic and some advanced technologies.
sla_notes_details: Students prepare land, prepare or obtain seedlings, plant at recommended spacing, apply manure or fertilizer, weed, prune, control pests and diseases and harvest at the right time. They implement affordable solutions to identified problems, such as using neem or ash as botanical pesticides, mulching to conserve moisture and training grape on simple trellises made from local poles. They try out technologies such as drip irrigation, grafting, integrated pest management and simple processing tools, and compare results with traditional practice. Records of inputs, labour and yields are kept for evaluation.
sla_notes_illustrations: Students at a school farm set up a small grape trellis, prune vines to two buds per spur, install a drip line and measure differences in growth against vines watered by hand.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skills help students start their own farms, join agribusiness firms and teach their families improved practices.
sla_exercise: Why is pruning of grapevines important?::It controls vine shape and improves fruit yield and quality.||Name one botanical pesticide.::Neem extract (or ash, chilli or tobacco solution).||Why compare improved and traditional practice?::To find out which method gives better yield and profit.

sla_notes_intro: Students practise managing goats and sheep at school or nearby farms using basic and advanced technologies.
sla_notes_details: Practices include building or improving housing, selecting animals, feeding balanced rations with pasture, browse, hay and supplements, providing clean water, routine health care (dipping, drenching, vaccination, hoof trimming), breeding management, kidding or lambing care, milking, shearing and record keeping. Students implement affordable solutions for problems such as feed shortage or parasites, for example growing fodder trees and rotating pastures, and try out technologies like artificial insemination, milk coolers or phone-based record keeping and adapt them to local conditions.
sla_notes_illustrations: Students plant Leucaena and Napier grass to feed the school goats in the dry season and record body weight monthly to compare with animals given only natural pasture.
sla_notes_daily_life: The practical skills prepare students to keep goats and sheep profitably for meat, milk or fibre.
sla_exercise: Name one fodder tree used for goats.::Leucaena (or Calliandra).||What routine practices keep goats and sheep healthy?::Dipping or spraying, drenching, vaccination and clean housing.||Why are records kept in an animal project?::To monitor growth, health, production and costs.

learning_activity_name: Complete and submit a report on the project started in Form V
sla_name: Completing and reporting the agriculture project
sla_assessment_criteria: The project started in Form V is well completed and a report submitted.
sla_teaching_aids: Various fields/ agencies involved in agricultural production|Various reports depicting projects done in segments of crop/animal production value chain
sla_references: TET(2023), AGRICULTURE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students finish the project started in Form V, present their work and submit a report.
sla_notes_details: Students complete the planned activities, collect final data on production, costs and income, and analyse the results to see whether the objectives were met. The report includes a title, introduction and objectives, methodology, results with tables and photographs, discussion, challenges and lessons learned, conclusions and recommendations. They present the project to teachers and classmates and respond to questions. The project is assessed by the criteria that were set at the start.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who kept broilers for six weeks records feed used, weight gain and sales, calculates a profit of the batch and presents it in a report with a chart and photographs.
sla_notes_daily_life: Completing and reporting projects builds discipline and communication skills used in farming, business and further studies.
sla_exercise: List three parts of a project report.::Introduction, methodology and results (also conclusion and recommendations).||How is project profit calculated?::Total income minus total costs.||Why is a presentation important after finishing a project?::It allows sharing of results and receiving feedback from others.
